subtitle: The wrong encoding quietly tells the model something false.

code:
ohe = OneHotEncoder(sparse=False, handle_unknown="ignore")
city_oh = ohe.fit_transform(df[["city"]])
print(ohe.get_feature_names_out(["city"]))
# ['city_Atlanta' 'city_Boston' 'city_Chicago']
ohe.transform(pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Denver"]}))   # [[0. 0. 0.]] -- unseen!
caption: handle_unknown="ignore" turns an unseen category into all zeros instead of an error.

steps.label: pd.get_dummies() DOESN'T REMEMBER
steps.sub: Risky for train/test consistency -- prefer sklearn

eyebrow: Ordinal encoding: state the order explicitly
caption: Without an explicit order, it defaults to alphabetical -- "premium" before "basic"!

eyebrow: The classic mistake: numbering a nominal column
code:
codes = OrdinalEncoder().fit_transform(df[["city"]])  # Atlanta=0, Boston=1, Chicago=2
m_ord = LinearRegression().fit(codes, y)
m_oh = LinearRegression().fit(city_oh, y)
print(round(m_ord.score(codes, y), 3))   # 0.04  -- a fake ordering
print(round(m_oh.score(city_oh, y), 3))  # 0.815 -- one-hot
caption: Same data, same target -- R² jumps 20x just from choosing the right encoding.

eyebrow: Boston can't be the highest if it's "in the middle"
caption: Real output: a fake 0-1-2 ordering forces a straight line through the three cities.
